description: Personal union of Denmark, Norway, and Sweden (1397–1523) assembled by Queen Margaret I of Denmark; dominated by Danish interests, it provoked recurrent Swedish rebellions culminating in the Stockholm Bloodbath (1520) and Gustavus Vasa's liberation (1523), which definitively ended Scandinavian unification and established the independent Swedish kingdom.

temporal.notes: Personal union; Swedish withdrawal recurring; full dissolution 1523

lifecycle_phases.description: Queen Margaret I of Denmark, regent for her nephew Eric of Pomerania, convenes the Union of Kalmar (1397), formally uniting Denmark, Norway, and Sweden under a single monarch. Margaret is the effective ruler, the most powerful woman in medieval northern Europe. She uses skillful diplomacy and controlled distribution of patronage to hold the three kingdoms together against constant aristocratic resistance.

After Margaret's death, successive Danish kings face constant Swedish rebellion; Sweden repeatedly secedes under the Sture regents (1470–1520). Danish King Christian II's brutal suppression of Swedish resistance at the Stockholm Bloodbath (1520), executing 80-90 Swedish nobles and clergy, triggers Gustav Vasa's rebellion and the permanent dissolution of the union (1523).

rise_factors.description: Margaret I's personal political genius, not any institutional advantage, held the union together; her ability to balance the competing interests of three nobilities, three churches, and three traditions within a single dynastic framework was a remarkable individual achievement

The union provided collective bargaining power against the Hanseatic League's commercial domination of Baltic trade; Danish control of the Sound tolls combined with Swedish iron and copper exports created negotiating leverage

Denmark's control of the Øresund strait between Sweden and modern Denmark gave the union control over all Baltic maritime trade; every ship passing paid tolls, making the Sound the most profitable toll station in Europe

Margaret I of Denmark united Denmark, Norway, and Sweden under a single monarch through the 1397 Treaty of Kalmar, ending decades of inter-Scandinavian warfare and creating the largest territorial state in European history at the time.
The combined naval power of the three Scandinavian kingdoms gave the union significant bargaining leverage against the Hanseatic League's dominance of Baltic trade, periodically forcing concessions.

decline_factors.description: The union was fundamentally a Danish dynastic project; Swedish and Norwegian nobles resisted the systematic favoritism shown to Danish clients in royal appointments; the structural imbalance made the union unstable from the start

Swedish nobility repeatedly resisted Danish domination; the Stockholm Bloodbath (1520), when Christian II executed Swedish nobles, catalyzed Gustav Vasa's successful independence war and permanently ended the Union in 1523

The three kingdoms retained separate laws, parliaments, and cultures; no central institution developed; the union existed as a personal connection through the monarch rather than a coherent state, making it vulnerable to succession disputes

Swedish nobles repeatedly rebelled against Danish-dominated union governance, viewing Copenhagen-centered rule as exploitative; the Stockholm Bloodbath of 1520 triggered the final Swedish secession under Gustav Vasa.

No joint institutions were ever established, each kingdom retained its own council and laws, meaning the union depended entirely on personal royal authority and collapsed when strong leadership was absent.
